claim: Piezo1 is the most highly expressed calcium channel among 78 calcium channels detected in MLO-Y4 cells under static condition.
source: Piezo1 was the most highly expressed among 78 calcium channels detected in MLO-Y4 cells under static condition (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: Piezo1 was highly up-regulated by fluid flow in MLO-Y4 cells as determined by RNA-seq.
source: In addition, Piezo1 was also highly up-regulated by fluid flow in MLO-Y4 cells as determined by RNA-seq (Figure 1A) and RT-qPCR (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 1A and RT-qPCR data in Figure 1B

claim: Piezo1 was highly up-regulated by fluid flow in MLO-Y4 cells as determined by RT-qPCR.
source: In addition, Piezo1 was also highly up-regulated by fluid flow in MLO-Y4 cells as determined by RNA-seq (Figure 1A) and RT-qPCR (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1B

claim: The expression of Piezo1 was approximately 200-fold higher than that of Piezo2 in MLO-Y4 cells.
source: Consistent with this previous evidence, the expression of Piezo1 was approximately 200-fold higher than that of Piezo2 in MLO-Y4 cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1B

claim: Piezo1 expression was much higher than Piezo2 in osteocyte-enriched cortical bone isolated from 12-week-old mice.
source: Piezo1 expression was also much higher than Piezo2 in osteocyte-enriched cortical bone isolated from 12-week-old mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1C

claim: Knock-down of Piezo1 mRNA in MLO-Y4 cells significantly blunted the increase in intracellular calcium induced by fluid-flow.
source: Knock-down of Piezo1 mRNA in MLO-Y4 cells significantly blunted the increase in intracellular calcium induced by fluid-flow (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by calcium flux measurements in Figure 1D

claim: Knock-down of Piezo1 blunted fluid-flow stimulation of Ptgs2.
source: Knock-down of Piezo1 also blunted fluid-flow stimulation of Ptgs2 and Tnfrsf11b (Figure 1E), two well-known targets of fluid shear stress in osteocytes (Wadhwa et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1E and cited literature

claim: Knock-down of Piezo1 blunted fluid-flow stimulation of Tnfrsf11b.
source: Knock-down of Piezo1 also blunted fluid-flow stimulation of Ptgs2 and Tnfrsf11b (Figure 1E), two well-known targets of fluid shear stress in osteocytes (Wadhwa et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1E and cited literature

claim: Ptgs2 is a well-known target of fluid shear stress in osteocytes.
source: Knock-down of Piezo1 also blunted fluid-flow stimulation of Ptgs2 and Tnfrsf11b (Figure 1E), two well-known targets of fluid shear stress in osteocytes (Wadhwa et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wadhwa et al., 2002 and Zhao et al., 2016

claim: Tnfrsf11b is a well-known target of fluid shear stress in osteocytes.
source: Knock-down of Piezo1 also blunted fluid-flow stimulation of Ptgs2 and Tnfrsf11b (Figure 1E), two well-known targets of fluid shear stress in osteocytes (Wadhwa et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wadhwa et al., 2002 and Zhao et al., 2016

claim: Overexpression of Piezo1 in MLO-Y4 cells increased the expression of Ptgs2.
source: Conversely, overexpression of Piezo1 in MLO-Y4 cells increased the expression of Ptgs2 and Tnfrsf11b and enhanced their induction by fluid shear stress (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1F

claim: Overexpression of Piezo1 in MLO-Y4 cells increased the expression of Tnfrsf11b.
source: Conversely, overexpression of Piezo1 in MLO-Y4 cells increased the expression of Ptgs2 and Tnfrsf11b and enhanced their induction by fluid shear stress (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1F

claim: Overexpression of Piezo1 in MLO-Y4 cells enhanced the induction of Ptgs2 by fluid shear stress.
source: Conversely, overexpression of Piezo1 in MLO-Y4 cells increased the expression of Ptgs2 and Tnfrsf11b and enhanced their induction by fluid shear stress (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1F

claim: Overexpression of Piezo1 in MLO-Y4 cells enhanced the induction of Tnfrsf11b by fluid shear stress.
source: Conversely, overexpression of Piezo1 in MLO-Y4 cells increased the expression of Ptgs2 and Tnfrsf11b and enhanced their induction by fluid shear stress (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 1F

claim: Piezo1 contributes to the response of MLO-Y4 cells to fluid shear stress.
source: These results demonstrate that Piezo1 contributes to the response of MLO-Y4 cells to fluid shear stress.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of knockdown and overexpression experiments

claim: Deletion of the Piezo1 gene was confirmed by qPCR of genomic DNA isolated from osteocyte-enriched cortical bone.
source: Deletion of the Piezo1 gene was confirmed by qPCR of genomic DNA isolated from osteocyte-enriched cortical bone (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 2A

claim: Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice exhibited normal body weight compared to their control Piezo1f/f littermates.
source: Mice lacking the Piezo1 gene in osteoblasts and osteocytes, hereafter referred to as Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice, exhibited normal body weight compared to their control Piezo1f/f littermates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Both female and male Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice exhibited low bone mineral density (BMD) at 5, 8, and 12 weeks of age as measured by dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA).
source: Both female and male Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice exhibited low bone mineral density (BMD) at 5, 8, and 12 weeks of age as measured by dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) and the difference increased as the mice matured (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by DXA measurements in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: The BMD difference between Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice and controls increased as the mice matured.
source: Both female and male Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice exhibited low bone mineral density (BMD) at 5, 8, and 12 weeks of age as measured by dual energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) and the difference increased as the mice matured (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by DXA measurements in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Spontaneous fractures were observed in the tibia of conditional knockout mice at a frequency of 0.16.
source: Spontaneous fractures were observed in the tibia of conditional knockout mice at a frequency of 0.16 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by X-ray images in Figure 2C

claim: Femoral cortical thickness was lower in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice compared with controls in both sexes.
source: Detailed analysis of the skeletal phenotype of these mice at 12 weeks of age by micro-CT revealed that femoral cortical thickness was lower in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice compared with controls in both sexes (Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: Periosteal circumference was decreased in the femur of Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice.
source: Periosteal and endocortical circumferences were also decreased in the femur of Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2E

claim: Endocortical circumference was decreased in the femur of Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice.
source: Periosteal and endocortical circumferences were also decreased in the femur of Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2E

claim: The total cross sectional area was reduced in the conditional knockout mice.
source: In line with these changes, the total cross sectional area, cortical bone area, and medullary area were reduced in the conditional knockout mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Cortical bone area was reduced in the conditional knockout mice.
source: In line with these changes, the total cross sectional area, cortical bone area, and medullary area were reduced in the conditional knockout mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Medullary area was reduced in the conditional knockout mice.
source: In line with these changes, the total cross sectional area, cortical bone area, and medullary area were reduced in the conditional knockout mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: The length of the femurs was not different between genotypes indicating that longitudinal bone growth was normal in conditional knockout mice.
source: In contrast to the changes in bone width, the length of the femurs was not different between genotypes indicating that longitudinal bone growth was normal in conditional knockout mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by femur length measurements in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: A decrease in cortical bone thickness was detected in vertebrae of Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f female and male mice.
source: A decrease in cortical bone thickness was also detected in vertebrae of Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f female and male mice (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: Bone volume over tissue volume was decreased in the femur of female Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice compared to their control littermates.
source: Analysis of cancellous bone in the femur and vertebra revealed that bone volume over tissue volume, trabecular number, and trabecular thickness were decreased, while trabecular separation was increased in female Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice compared to their control littermates (Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H

claim: Trabecular number was decreased in the femur of female Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice compared to their control littermates.
source: Analysis of cancellous bone in the femur and vertebra revealed that bone volume over tissue volume, trabecular number, and trabecular thickness were decreased, while trabecular separation was increased in female Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice compared to their control littermates (Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H

evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H

evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H

evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H

source: Similar results were obtained in male mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I,J

claim: The femurs from Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice had reduced stiffness.
source: Biomechanical testing by 3-point bending showed that the femurs from Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice had reduced stiffness and ultimate force (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by biomechanical testing data in Figure 2I

claim: The femurs from Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice had reduced ultimate force.
source: Biomechanical testing by 3-point bending showed that the femurs from Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice had reduced stiffness and ultimate force (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by biomechanical testing data in Figure 2I

claim: The Young's modulus did not change in femurs from Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice.
source: However, the Young's modulus and ultimate stress did not change, suggesting that the lower strength was due to differences in size and mass rather than changes in bone material properties (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by biomechanical testing data in Figure 2I

claim: The ultimate stress did not change in femurs from Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice.
source: However, the Young's modulus and ultimate stress did not change, suggesting that the lower strength was due to differences in size and mass rather than changes in bone material properties (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by biomechanical testing data in Figure 2I

claim: The lower strength in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice was due to differences in size and mass rather than changes in bone material properties.
source: However, the Young's modulus and ultimate stress did not change, suggesting that the lower strength was due to differences in size and mass rather than changes in bone material properties (Figure 2I).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Young's modulus and ultimate stress did not change

claim: The tissue mineral density of femoral cortical bone was unaffected by deletion of Piezo1.
source: Consistent with this, the tissue mineral density of femoral cortical bone was unaffected by deletion of Piezo1 (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by tissue mineral density measurements in Figure 2J

claim: Periosteal mineralizing surface was significantly reduced in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice at 5 weeks.
source: To evaluate the cellular changes underlying the skeletal phenotype of the conditional knockout mice, we performed bone histomorphometry of femoral cortical bone and found that periosteal and endocortical mineralizing surfaces were significantly reduced in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice at 5 weeks, an age of rapid bone growth (Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometry data in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: Endocortical mineralizing surface was significantly reduced in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice at 5 weeks.
source: To evaluate the cellular changes underlying the skeletal phenotype of the conditional knockout mice, we performed bone histomorphometry of femoral cortical bone and found that periosteal and endocortical mineralizing surfaces were significantly reduced in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice at 5 weeks, an age of rapid bone growth (Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometry data in Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A

claim: Double labels were not observed in the conditional knockout mice, indicating that the bone formation rate at the periosteum of Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice was extremely low.
source: While double labels were easily seen in control mice, double labels were not observed in the conditional knockout mice, indicating that the bone formation rate at the periosteum of Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice was extremely low.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of double labels in histomorphometry

claim: Mineralizing surface was decreased in vertebral trabecular bone of the conditional knockout mice.
source: Histomorphometric analysis of vertebral trabecular bone also revealed a decrease in mineralizing surface, mineral apposition rate, and bone formation rate in the conditional knockout mice (Figure 2L).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometry data in Figure 2L

claim: Mineral apposition rate was decreased in vertebral trabecular bone of the conditional knockout mice.
source: Histomorphometric analysis of vertebral trabecular bone also revealed a decrease in mineralizing surface, mineral apposition rate, and bone formation rate in the conditional knockout mice (Figure 2L).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometry data in Figure 2L

claim: Bone formation rate was decreased in vertebral trabecular bone of the conditional knockout mice.
source: Histomorphometric analysis of vertebral trabecular bone also revealed a decrease in mineralizing surface, mineral apposition rate, and bone formation rate in the conditional knockout mice (Figure 2L).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometry data in Figure 2L

claim: Osteoblast number was lower in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice.
source: In line with these changes, osteoblast number was lower in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice (Figure 2M).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometry data in Figure 2M

claim: An increase in osteoclast number was observed in the conditional knockout mice.
source: In addition, we observed an increase in osteoclast number in the conditional knockout mice (Figure 2M).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometry data in Figure 2M

claim: The percentage of empty osteocyte lacunae was not changed in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice compared to their littermate controls.
source: We did not observe changes in the percentage of empty osteocyte lacunae or the number of osteocytes normalized to bone area in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice compared to their littermate controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C

claim: The number of osteocytes normalized to bone area was not changed in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice compared to their littermate controls.
source: We did not observe changes in the percentage of empty osteocyte lacunae or the number of osteocytes normalized to bone area in Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice compared to their littermate controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C

claim: No apparent morphological changes in osteocytes were observed in the conditional knockout mice.
source: Consistent with these results, we did not observe any apparent morphological changes in osteocytes in the conditional knockout mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by histological images in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D

claim: Knock-down of Piezo1 in MLO-Y4 cells decreased Capase3 activity.
source: In addition, knock-down of Piezo1 in MLO-Y4 cells decreased, rather than increased, Capase3 activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by Caspase3 activity measurements in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E

claim: Piezo1 deletion does not increase osteocyte death in vitro or in vivo.
source: These results indicate that Piezo1 deletion does not increase osteocyte death in vitro or in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of changes in empty lacunae, osteocyte number, and Caspase3 activity

claim: Osteoblast differentiation of bone marrow stromal cells from Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice was normal, as indicated by Alizarin Red staining.
source: We also analyzed osteoblastogenesis in vitro and found normal osteoblast differentiation of bone marrow stromal cells from Dmp1-Cre;Piezo1f/f mice, as indicated by Alizarin Red staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: Supported by Alizarin Red staining in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F

claim: About 20% deletion of the Piezo1 gene was detected in gastrocnemius muscle of the conditional knockout mice.
source: We detected about 20% deletion of the Piezo1 gene in the conditional knockout mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A

claim: Piezo1 expression in gastrocnemius muscle was about 10 times lower than that in bone.
source: In addition, Piezo1 expression in gastrocnemius muscle was about 10 times lower than that in bone (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B

claim: No difference in lean body weight was observed between the conditional knockout mice and their control littermates.
source: More importantly, we did not observe any difference in lean body weight or gastrocnemius muscle mass between the conditional knockout mice and their control littermates (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D

claim: No difference in gastrocnemius muscle mass was observed between the conditional knockout mice and their control littermates.
source: More importantly, we did not observe any difference in lean body weight or gastrocnemius muscle mass between the conditional knockout mice and their control littermates (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by muscle mass measurements in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D

claim: Piezo1 in osteoblasts, osteocytes, or both, is essential for normal bone size and mass.
source: These results demonstrate that Piezo1 in osteoblasts, osteocytes, or both, is essential for normal bone size and mass.
evidence: Inferred from the combined skeletal phenotype data

claim: Two weeks of anabolic loading increased tibial cortical thickness in control mice but not in conditional knockout mice.
source: Two weeks of anabolic loading increased tibial cortical thickness in control mice but not in conditional knockout mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 3B

claim: Loading increased periosteal bone formation rate in control mice, due to increases in both mineralizing surface and mineral apposition rate.
source: Consistent with the changes in bone mass, loading increased periosteal bone formation rate in control mice, due to increases in both mineralizing surface and mineral apposition rate (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometry data in Figure 3C,D

claim: The load-stimulated bone formation was significantly blunted in conditional knockout mice.
source: The load-stimulated bone formation was significantly blunted in conditional knockout mice (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by histomorphometry data in Figure 3C,D

claim: Piezo1 in osteoblasts, osteocytes, or both, plays an essential role in the response of the skeleton to mechanical loads.
source: These results suggest that Piezo1 in osteoblasts, osteocytes, or both, plays an essential role in the response of the skeleton to mechanical loads.
evidence: Inferred from the blunted response to mechanical loading in conditional knockout mice

claim: Wnt1 mRNA was lower in cortical bone shafts of conditional knockout mice at both 5 and 12 weeks of age.
source: Wnt1 mRNA was lower in cortical bone shafts of conditional knockout mice at both 5 and 12 weeks of age while the expression of Sost was unaffected (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4A,B

claim: The expression of Sost was unaffected in cortical bone shafts of conditional knockout mice at both 5 and 12 weeks of age.
source: Wnt1 mRNA was lower in cortical bone shafts of conditional knockout mice at both 5 and 12 weeks of age while the expression of Sost was unaffected (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4A,B

claim: Expression of RANKL (Tnfsf11) was higher in the conditional knockout mice.
source: Consistent with increased osteoclast number, expression of the essential pro-osteoclastogenic cytokine RANKL (Tnfsf11) was higher in the conditional knockout mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4B

claim: Expression of OPG (Tnfrsf11b) was not different between the genotypes.
source: In contrast, expression of OPG (Tnfrsf11b), a secreted decoy receptor for RANKL, was not different between the genotypes (Figure 4B), despite our observation of reduced Tnfrsf11b expression in MLO-Y4 cells lacking Piezo1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4B

claim: Fluid shear stress increased Wnt1 expression in MLO-Y4 cells but this was blunted after knock-down of Piezo1.
source: Fluid shear stress increased Wnt1 expression in MLO-Y4 cells but this was blunted after knock-down of Piezo1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4C

claim: Basal expression of Wnt1 was reduced by Piezo1 knock-down.
source: Basal expression of Wnt1 was also reduced by Piezo1 knock-down (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4C

claim: Piezo1 has been shown to control YAP1 and TAZ activity.
source: YAP1 and TAZ are two related transcriptional cofactors that can be activated by mechanical signals, including fluid flow and matrix rigidity, and recently Piezo1 has been shown to control their activity (Wang et al., 2016; Dupont et al., 2011; Pathak et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2016; Dupont et al., 2011; Pathak et al., 2014

claim: Deletion of Yap1 and Taz using Dmp1-Cre decreases bone mass, due to both reduced bone formation and increased osteoclast number.
source: We have shown previously that deletion of Yap1 and Taz using Dmp1-Cre decreases bone mass, due to both reduced bone formation and increased osteoclast number (Xiong et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xiong et al., 2018

claim: Cortical thickness was significantly decreased in Dmp1-Cre;Yap1f/f,Tazf/f mice compared to their Yap1f/f,Tazf/f littermates.
source: Here, we analyzed the diaphysis of femurs of these mice and found that cortical thickness, periosteal circumference, and endocortical circumference were significantly decreased in Dmp1-Cre;Yap1f/f,Tazf/f mice compared to their Yap1f/f,Tazf/f littermates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Periosteal circumference was significantly decreased in Dmp1-Cre;Yap1f/f,Tazf/f mice compared to their Yap1f/f,Tazf/f littermates.
source: Here, we analyzed the diaphysis of femurs of these mice and found that cortical thickness, periosteal circumference, and endocortical circumference were significantly decreased in Dmp1-Cre;Yap1f/f,Tazf/f mice compared to their Yap1f/f,Tazf/f littermates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Endocortical circumference was significantly decreased in Dmp1-Cre;Yap1f/f,Tazf/f mice compared to their Yap1f/f,Tazf/f littermates.
source: Here, we analyzed the diaphysis of femurs of these mice and found that cortical thickness, periosteal circumference, and endocortical circumference were significantly decreased in Dmp1-Cre;Yap1f/f,Tazf/f mice compared to their Yap1f/f,Tazf/f littermates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by micro-CT data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Silencing the Piezo1 gene in MLO-Y4 cells decreased the expression of Cyr61.
source: Silencing the Piezo1 gene in MLO-Y4 cells decreased the expression of Cyr61, a YAP1 and TAZ target gene, and blunted fluid shear stress induction of Cyr61 expression (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4C

claim: Silencing the Piezo1 gene in MLO-Y4 cells blunted fluid shear stress induction of Cyr61 expression.
source: Silencing the Piezo1 gene in MLO-Y4 cells decreased the expression of Cyr61, a YAP1 and TAZ target gene, and blunted fluid shear stress induction of Cyr61 expression (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4C

claim: Lack of Yap1 and Taz blunted the response to fluid flow including the increase in Ptgs2 expression.
source: We then silenced the Yap1 and Taz genes in MLO-Y4 cells to examine whether these factors are required for the stimulation of Wnt1 by fluid shear stress. We found that lack of Yap1 and Taz blunted the response to fluid flow including the increase in Ptgs2, Wnt1, and Cyr61 expression (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4D

claim: Lack of Yap1 and Taz blunted the response to fluid flow including the increase in Wnt1 expression.
source: We then silenced the Yap1 and Taz genes in MLO-Y4 cells to examine whether these factors are required for the stimulation of Wnt1 by fluid shear stress. We found that lack of Yap1 and Taz blunted the response to fluid flow including the increase in Ptgs2, Wnt1, and Cyr61 expression (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4D

claim: Lack of Yap1 and Taz blunted the response to fluid flow including the increase in Cyr61 expression.
source: We then silenced the Yap1 and Taz genes in MLO-Y4 cells to examine whether these factors are required for the stimulation of Wnt1 by fluid shear stress. We found that lack of Yap1 and Taz blunted the response to fluid flow including the increase in Ptgs2, Wnt1, and Cyr61 expression (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data in Figure 4D
